text: When David had gone a little beyond the summit, there was Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant, coming to meet him with a pair of saddled donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a skin of wine.

The king asked Ziba, "What are these for?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and the summer fruits are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for those who grow faint in the wilderness to drink."

versions.text: The king asked Ziba, "What are these for?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and the summer fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for those who grow faint in the wilderness to drink."
versions.explanation: Verse 1 speaks of 'a hundred summer fruits' (plural); using the singular 'summer fruit' here creates an inconsistency for a listener hearing the two verses read in succession. Matching the plural keeps the inventory clear.

text: "And where is your master's son?" the king asked. Ziba said to the king, "He is staying in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will restore my father's kingdom to me.'"
Then the king said to Ziba, "Everything that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." Ziba said, "I bow before you. May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king."
As King David approached Bahurim, a man came out from there, from the clan of the house of Saul. His name was Shimei son of Gera, and he came out cursing as he went.
He pelted David and all King David's servants with stones, though all the troops and all the warriors were on his right and on his left.
This is what Shimei said as he cursed: "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man!

The LORD has brought back upon you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has handed the kingdom over to your son Absalom. See, disaster has overtaken you, because you are a man of blood!"

versions.text: The LORD has brought back upon you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has handed the kingdom over to your son Absalom. Now you are caught in your own evil, because you are a man of blood!"
versions.explanation: 'Caught in' adds an image not present in the Hebrew, which says simply 'behold, you are in your calamity.' The suggested wording keeps the accusation while reading more naturally aloud and staying closer to the sense of רָעָה as the ruin now falling on David.

versions.text: See, disaster has overtaken you, because you are a man of blood!"
versions.explanation: Two full clauses of Shimei's curse are missing: the LORD repaying the blood of Saul's house on David, and the giving of the kingdom into Absalom's hand. Without them the verse loses the accusation that motivates the whole speech and the pronoun 'you' has no stated charge. The closing clause is kept as revised, since the earlier note rightly avoided 'caught in your own evil.'

text: Then Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head."
But the king said, "What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, for the LORD has told him, 'Curse David.' Who then can ask, 'Why have you done this?'"

versions.text: But the king said, "What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? If he curses because the LORD has told him, 'Curse David,' who then can ask, 'Why have you done this?'"
versions.explanation: The reading of the Hebrew text here (כֹּה יְקַלֵּל) is a permissive statement, 'let him curse thus,' not a conditional 'if he curses.' David is granting permission, which is the point of the whole speech (compare verse 11, 'let him curse'). The conditional rendering weakens David's deliberate submission to the LORD's hand and also turns the following clause into an awkward dependent chain.

text: And David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Look, my own son, my own flesh and blood, is seeking my life. How much more, then, this Benjaminite! Leave him alone and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to.
Perhaps the LORD will look on my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today."
So David and his men went on their way, while Shimei kept pace with him along the hillside opposite, cursing as he went, throwing stones at him and flinging dust.
The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted, and there he refreshed himself.
Meanwhile Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.
When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, he said to him, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"
Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why didn't you go with your friend?"
Hushai answered Absalom, "No. The one chosen by the LORD, by this people, and by all the men of Israel—his I will be, and with him I will stay.
And furthermore, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I served your father, so I will serve you."
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give us your counsel. What should we do?"

Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he left to keep the house. Then all Israel will hear that you have made yourself odious to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened."
So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.
Now in those days the counsel Ahithophel gave was regarded as though one had inquired of the word of God—so was all Ahithophel's counsel esteemed by both David and Absalom.
